desc:
The array nums has length n and every element lies in the range 1..n. Values may repeat any number of times, so some numbers of 1..n may not appear at all. Return all numbers in 1..n that do not appear in nums, in ascending order (an empty array if every number appears).

Example: nums = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1] returns [5, 6].
hints: A set of the values, compared with 1..n, gives the answer. Can you keep the bookkeeping inside nums?
Because every value is a valid position (shifted by one), you can use position v - 1 to say "v is present", for example by making that entry negative.
After marking all values, every position that is still positive corresponds to a number that never occurred: position i stands for the number i + 1.
editorial: Use the array as its own presence table. For every element take v = abs(x) and force nums[v - 1] to be negative (using -abs(...) so that repeated values do not flip it back). When the pass is finished, an index whose entry is still positive was never pointed to, so the number i + 1 is missing.

The scan runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space apart from the output. The result is produced in ascending order automatically because we read the indices left to right. A hash-set solution is equally fast but needs O(n) memory.
